title: Plan the load test for the inference endpoint before the launch date
body:
Launching without knowing where the endpoint falls over would be a bet I do not need to make, and a load test run carelessly is nearly as bad because it either proves nothing or takes the shared staging cluster down for everybody. So plan it on paper first.

Start from the traffic estimate: expected peak requests per second, the ratio of short to long prompts, and the latency target at the 95th and 99th percentile. Build the test from replayed real request shapes, not a uniform synthetic prompt, since token length drives GPU time far more than request count. Ramp in steps, hold each step long enough for queues to settle, and record where p99 bends upward, which is the number I actually want. Then work out the cost: instance hours for the test, the price per hour of the GPU type, and how long the run will take including warm-up and one rerun. Agree the window with whoever shares staging, and set a hard stop on spend so a runaway script cannot eat the month's budget. Finish with a one-paragraph capacity statement: replicas needed at peak with 30 percent headroom. [[obsidian:Load testing plan]]

title: Apply rate-distortion intuition to decide how far to compress embeddings
body:
I have been treating embedding compression as a search for the smallest size that still works, which hides that this is a curve and not a threshold. Rate-distortion theory says that for a given amount of tolerated distortion there is a minimum number of bits, and that each extra bit buys less than the one before. If that holds for my vectors, the first halving of memory should be nearly free and the last one should hurt badly, and I should be able to see the knee.

Test that on a real set. Take a sample of a hundred thousand embeddings, compress them at 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1 bits per dimension, and for each compute two things: mean squared reconstruction error, and recall at 10 against exact search on the originals. Plot both against bits per dimension. The interesting question is whether reconstruction error and recall agree about where the knee is, because I suspect recall is far more forgiving, since it only needs the ranking preserved rather than the vectors. Also try a dimension-truncated version at equal total bits, to see whether spending bits on fewer dimensions or fewer bits on all dimensions gives the better trade. Finish with a paragraph saying which operating point I would pick and why.

title: Stop hardcoding the Spanish dictionary and make the lookup language-agnostic
body: Every lookup in the app currently assumes the headword is Spanish: the parser expects one particular entry format, the accent stripping is baked in, and the sort order is Spanish too. The first task is to list which of those would actually trigger an alert today and which would only be found by a customer.

Then read a few public runbooks and postmortem templates, and work out what a runbook for a model incident needs that a service runbook does not. My guess: how to roll back to the previous model version, how to switch to a fallback rule, who can decide that a degraded model is better than no model, and how to tell a data problem from a model problem in the first ten minutes.

End with a draft one-page runbook for a single made-up ranking service and a blameless postmortem outline with a section for what the monitoring failed to notice. The goal is to discuss severity levels and escalation paths for ML systems without borrowing vocabulary that does not fit.

body: The dashboard shows high GPU utilization while the run is plainly slow, which is the classic illusion: the metric only says a kernel was resident, not that the tensor cores were busy. title: Build a location-scouting routine, then compare it with the result
body:
Good light at a location is mostly a matter of homework, and I have been doing the homework in my head, which means I forget it by the time I arrive. Make a short template, one entry per place: where the sun will be at the hour I plan to be there, what the weather forecast says for that day, and the shot I expect to get, described in a sentence or a rough sketch.

The useful step is the last one. After the outing, put the actual frame next to the prediction and write two lines on what differed: the light came from another angle, the cloud did something unexpected, the composition I imagined was blocked by a fence. After five or six entries I should see which part of my planning is consistently wrong, and that is the part to fix. Start with one place I already know well, so the comparison is about the method and not about an unfamiliar spot.

title: Write down the four judge biases and one cheap mitigation for each

title: Design exceptions in Python with chaining and exception groups
body:
My current habit is catching Exception near the top and logging a string, which throws away exactly the information I would want later. Learn the alternatives properly. First, a small hierarchy for one project: a base error for the package and two or three specific subclasses, with a clear rule for when to create a new class and when an existing built-in is right.

body:
There are two broad ways to deal with position bias in a tree ranker, and I have only ever used the cheap one. The cheap one is to add position as a feature at training time and set it to a constant at serving time, which works surprisingly often but quietly assumes the position effect is separable from relevance. The other is to learn propensities and reweight the loss, as in the inverse propensity scoring papers, or to learn relevance and examination jointly with a two-tower or regression-EM setup.

Pick the ranker we already have and write down which of these it does, if any. *The key question is whether the position feature leaks into the relevance score at serving time*, because if it does then every offline gain I have seen is partly the bias feeding itself. Then check what the library gives me: LightGBM has =lambdarank= with position debiasing arguments, and I should read what those actually do rather than trusting the parameter name. The fix is to make the check automatic and boring, so it runs whether or not I feel careful that day.

Plan: keep the golden set in the repo as a versioned file with question, expected key facts and the source passage it should cite. On every pull request, run the whole set through the candidate pipeline at temperature zero, score with a mix of cheap deterministic checks (citation present, key facts contained, no forbidden phrases) and a small judge-model rubric for the rest, and compare against the last released baseline instead of an absolute number. *Fail the build on any drop in the must-pass subset, and on a drop beyond the noise band for the rest.* Measure that noise band first by running the unchanged system ten times, since judge scores wobble. body: I can recite the DDPM training loss and still could not explain why it is the same thing as score matching, which means I have memorised a recipe rather than understood it. title: Read a full regression summary line by line and diagnose the multicollinearity
body:
I can fit an OLS model in a line of code but the summary table still reads like a wall of numbers, and I skip straight to the R-squared and the p-values. Fix that by generating data where two predictors are strongly correlated, say correlation 0.95 with the true effect split between them, and fitting the model with both, then with one at a time.

Go through the output row by row and write next to each number what it is for: coefficient, standard error, t, p, the confidence interval, the condition number warning at the bottom, the Durbin-Watson and Omnibus lines. Then compute the variance inflation factors by hand and check they match the library. The thing to see is that *the overall fit stays excellent while individual coefficients become wide and unstable*, and that refitting on fresh samples flips their signs. Repeat five hundred times and plot the coefficient estimates as a scatter, which should show a long diagonal cloud. Save the annotated summary as a one-page note for later reference.

title: Make the payment-calling agent safe to retry without double charging
body:
The agent calls an API that has real side effects, and at the moment a timeout means I cannot tell whether the call happened. If the loop just retries, I will eventually create a duplicate. Learn how idempotency keys work properly: who generates them, how long the server remembers them, and what happens when the same key arrives with a different payload.

Then the retry side. Exponential backoff with full jitter, a cap on attempts per call, and a global retry budget so that a bad hour downstream does not turn into a retry storm from my side. Start with a budget of roughly =10%= of request volume and see whether that is sensible. Write the key derivation as a small function that hashes task id plus step number, so a resumed run reuses the same key instead of minting a new one. Finish with a test that kills the process mid-call and checks that only one side effect lands.

title: Compare response-level, on-policy and self-distillation and note where each wins
body: The word distillation covers at least four different things, and the differences decide which one to reach for. title: Map what changed in C++ from C++11 to C++23 for my old habits
body:
My mental baseline is roughly C++11 with some C++14 sprinkled in, and I suspect I am writing around features that now exist. Make one table with a row per standard and only the changes I would realistically use, not the whole standards document.

For C++14 and 17 I want structured bindings, std::optional, std::variant, string_view, if with initialiser, fold expressions and guaranteed copy elision. For C++20, concepts, ranges, spans, three-way comparison and std::format, plus a note on coroutines that says whether I will ever need them or just need to recognise them. For C++23, std::expected as value-based error handling, since it is the one that could replace my exception habits, and std::print. Next to every row put the old idiom it replaces, so the table doubles as a list of things to stop writing.

After that, take one of my older small programs and modernise it using only what is in the table, then compare the two versions. If the result is not clearly shorter or clearer, the feature does not go on my regular list. Check what my compiler and standard library actually support before trusting the table, because support for the newer library features still lags behind the language ones.

title: Explain idempotency keys without hand-waving about retries
body: Every payment-style API I use says to send a key, and I could not say where the key is stored, for how long, or what happens on a crash between the charge and the write. Sketch the *store the key and the result in the same transaction* pattern on paper and walk one failure through it.

title: Set up seeding and deterministic training and record what still drifts
body:
Goal is a training script where the same seed gives the same curve on the same machine, and a written list of the reasons it will not do so elsewhere. Seed Python, NumPy and torch, set the cuBLAS workspace variable, turn on deterministic algorithms, and make the dataloader workers derive their seeds from the base seed instead of the clock.

Then run the same config twice and diff the loss logs line by line. I expect the first divergence to come from something like an atomic-add kernel or a nondeterministic op in the environment, not from my own code, and the point of the exercise is to find which. Put the result in =repro-notes.org= with the exact versions of torch, CUDA and the driver next to it, because bitwise equality across hardware or library versions is not something I should promise anyone, including myself. If the runs are identical for 1000 steps but diverge after that, note the step count rather than calling it fixed.

title: Add a rule to the agent file about never spinning up paid cloud resources
body: One line in the instruction file: ask first before creating anything that bills by the hour.

title: Compare DPO and its variants by the instability each one targets
body:
I keep lumping DPO, IPO, KTO and SimPO together as one thing, and I could not say why any of them exist beyond the original. Make a small table with one row per method and three columns: what the loss looks like, what failure it addresses, and what it costs.
Start from DPO and the implicit reward derived from the KL-regularised objective, then note the known problem that both chosen and rejected log-probabilities can drop together, and that the method can overfit when preferences are near-deterministic. IPO is meant to address that with a squared loss. KTO works from unpaired good and bad labels. SimPO removes the reference model and uses length-normalised log-probability. For each, find one sentence in the original paper that states the motivation, and copy it into the table so I am not paraphrasing from memory.
Then decide which of the four I would try first on a small model with a noisy preference set, and why. If there is time, run the cheapest one on a tiny dataset and watch the reward margin during training.

Why watch time is used for ranking instead of click-through, and how weighted logistic regression gets at it. What the example age feature is doing about the bias toward old videos. Why they hold out the most recent watch rather than a random one, which is the same leakage worry I have with my own offline evaluations.

Finish with two or three sentences on what I would say if asked in an interview why a two-stage system is used at all. The latency and catalogue-size argument is the one I tend to fumble, so write that one out in full and check the numbers against the paper.

title: Understand hybrid sparse and dense retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion
body: Compare BM25, vectors and a fused ranking on a few real queries. [[obsidian:Hybrid Retrieval Notes]]

title: Decide whether a second compact daypack is worth having
body: One for the city and one for hikes seems excessive, but swapping the contents every morning is what makes me skip the good bag. Compare weights and decide on one purchase. Notes live in [[obsidian:Travel gear wishlist]].

title: Replace the expired first aid kit and the dead whistle
Write down what each coding benchmark really tests and where it leaks
body: HumanEval, MBPP, SWE-bench and LiveCodeBench are quoted as if they were interchangeable, and they are not. For each one, write a short entry covering the task format, how the answers are checked, whether the test suite is weak enough to pass wrong code, and whether the problems have been public long enough to be in training data. Mark HumanEval as saturated, and note that =LiveCodeBench= tries to dodge contamination by using date-stamped problems. Finish with one line on which I would trust for a model released this year.

title: Compare linear attention variants against softmax attention on paper
body: Write out the kernel-feature view and the recurrent form for each variant, side by side. [[obsidian:Sequence Model Cheatsheet]]

title: Read up on indirect prompt injection through retrieved web pages
Learn how postings lists get compressed and why it makes queries faster
body: The claim that smaller indexes are also faster still sounds backwards to me, so I want to see it properly. Start with delta encoding of document IDs, then variable-byte, then the block-based schemes like PForDelta and Elias-Fano, and note what each one costs in decode speed and what it gives in space. Then look at skip pointers and how block-max metadata lets WAND or MaxScore skip whole blocks without decoding them. Finish by writing a toy postings list in Python, compressing it two ways and timing intersections on a few thousand terms.

title: Compare a ViT and a small ConvNet as the training set shrinks
body: The claim I keep reading is that transformers need far more data before they beat convolutions, and I would like to see the crossover myself rather than repeat it. Train a small ViT and a small ResNet-style net on CIFAR-10 using the same augmentation and the same optimizer settings, then repeat with 10%, 25% and 50% of the training set. Plot test accuracy against data size for both families and note where the curves cross, if they do. Afterwards change one thing in the recipe, such as stronger augmentation or longer training for the ViT, and see how far the gap moves. Write down parameter counts so the comparison is fair.

title: Write manual data parallelism by hand before touching DDP
body: Average gradients with all_reduce after backward on a toy MLP and compare the loss curve with a single process. [[obsidian:Distributed Training Exercises]]

title: Decide the randomization unit for the checkout-page test and defend it in writing
body: User-level randomization looks obvious, but people share accounts and switch devices, and if the change affects inventory or shipping promises, treated and control users are competing for the same stock. Write a one-page argument comparing user, session and region-level assignment: what each protects against, what it costs in power, and which interference I can live with. Add a note on stratifying by past order frequency so the heavy buyers do not land unevenly in one arm. The point is to have the choice on paper before the data exists, so I cannot rationalize it afterwards. See [[obsidian:Experiment design checklist]]

title: Check the music library against complete orchestra discographies for gaps
body: Compare my folders for my favourite orchestras with their full discographies and list *which recordings are missing* by year.

title: Implement PPO from scratch and match the CleanRL CartPole curve
body: I can explain the clipped objective but I have never written the whole loop, and the gaps show whenever I read RL code. Write a single-file PPO with GAE for CartPole, run five seeds, and overlay the return curve on the CleanRL reference until they agree within noise. [[obsidian:RL from scratch notes]]

title: Write out the NDCG formula and its common variants
body: I keep mixing up the linear-gain and exponential-gain versions of DCG, and I forget how ties and missing judgements are handled. Write both formulas with a five-item example, then note which library uses which so the numbers stop surprising me.

title: Read how =vLLM= schedules requests with continuous batching
body: Continuous batching is the reason throughput numbers look so different from naive serving.

title: Work out a latency and cost budget for a multi-stage ranker
body:
A ranking stack only makes sense once each stage has a number attached to it, so sketch one on paper.
- Set a total latency target and split it across retrieval, light ranking and heavy ranking
- Estimate cost per thousand requests for each stage at a given candidate count
- Find which stage to shrink first when the budget is blown

title: Watch one video of the *evolution simulation* channel and take notes
body: Write down what the simulation shows that a static diagram cannot.

title: Read one book on attention and change exactly one habit
body: My afternoons dissolve into tabs and chat notifications, and I only notice at the end. Pick a single short book on attention management, /Deep Work/ or something similar, read it over two weeks and change one thing, probably notifications off until noon.

title: Clean up the career notes folder and make a real preparation hub
body: The folder has one stub called =career.org= and a pile of loose files beside it. Move everything under it, link the question bank, stories and company notes from the stub, and delete whatever I have not opened in a year.

title: Learn how to test a system whose outputs change every run
body: Ordinary assertions break the moment the output is a sampled sentence or a model retrained on fresh data. I need a working vocabulary for this: fixed seeds and their limits, property-based checks, tolerance bands on metrics, golden sets with graded rather than exact matches, and using a second model as a judge with its own known biases. Also work out what belongs in CI versus a nightly run, since the expensive evals cannot gate every commit. Write a short note on one concrete test strategy for an LLM summariser: what is checked deterministically, what statistically, and what only a human reviews.

title: Learn what a good CLI tool schema looks like for agents
body: Read a few public tool-schema examples and note what makes parameter names and error messages easy for a model to use.

title: Sort out the tango music folder before it gets any worse
body: Half the files are named by whatever the download called them, so the same tanda shows up under three spellings. Fix the tags for orchestra, singer and year on one orchestra at a time, starting with the smallest folder, so the job actually gets finished.

title: Start a decision journal for every architecture call I make
body: Log each decision with the options considered, the *expected outcome and a date to check it*, then review quarterly.

title: Explain grokking precisely enough to stop saying it just generalizes late
body: The claim is that validation accuracy jumps long after training accuracy hits 100% on small algorithmic tasks. Read the original paper and write one paragraph on what /weight decay/ does to that story, with no hand-waving about phases.

title: Study how latent world models like Dreamer roll out imagined futures
body: Planning inside a learned latent model is the bit that makes sample efficiency plausible for robotics. Read the Dreamer v3 paper, then sketch the recurrent state-space model and where the reward head attaches. [[obsidian:World Models Reading List]]

title: Set *CPU and memory limits* on the workload and provoke an OOM kill
body: Set requests and limits, then deliberately exceed the memory limit once to see it fail.

title: Read a tutorial on unbiased learning to rank end to end
body: Pick one conference tutorial and work through the position-bias estimation part with the slides open.

title: Put paired tests and confidence intervals on the LLM comparisons
body: Last month's model comparison was one accuracy number each on 400 questions, and I called it a win. Redo it with a paired bootstrap on per-question correctness, report a 95% interval on the difference, and work out how many questions I would need to detect a 2-point gap.

title: Work through Bonferroni, Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg on last month's dashboard tests
body: We ran about thirty metric comparisons on one experiment and celebrated the two that came out under 0.05, which is close to what chance alone would hand us. Take the actual p-values and apply all three corrections, then see which results survive each. The choice should follow the cost of errors: for a launch decision where a false win is expensive, use Holm and control family-wise error; for exploratory metrics that only generate follow-up ideas, false discovery rate is fine. Write the rule down as a short paragraph that I can point at next time someone asks why a result was not called significant.

title: Read Thinking, Fast and Slow and mark which claims still hold
body:
Everyone quotes it and I have absorbed most of it second-hand, which is exactly the problem: I cannot say which parts I have actually checked. Several of the priming studies in the early chapters got caught up in the replication trouble, while loss aversion and the planning fallacy seem to have fared much better. Get a summary first, then read only the chapters on anchoring, the planning fallacy and the two-systems framing, and skip the long middle on prospect theory unless the summary says it earns the time.

While reading, keep a two-column list: claims with solid replications, and claims that rest on one small study. *The point is a sorted list of what still holds, not a book report.* Then look up the replication status of the three shakiest ones before writing anything down, and finish with one paragraph on what I would change in how I make estimates at work.

title: Compare batch norm, layer norm and no norm on one small net
body:
Use the same small convnet and seed for each, and change only the normalization layer.
- Plot training loss and the activation mean and std per layer
- Repeat with a learning rate ten times higher to see which variant *tolerates the larger step* best
- Try batch size 8 as well, since batch norm should suffer there

title: Watch one comprehensible-input video a day at a slightly too hard level
body: Pick =Dreaming Spanish= intermediate videos even if I only catch about half of each one.

title: Write down the shot types the pocket camera can pull off
body: Low angles, close macro, long exposures on a wall, and self-timer group shots are a start.

title: Study how a standard lakehouse platform is put together
body: Read up on Delta Lake or Iceberg, since *the transaction log* is what makes the rest of the platform make sense.

title: Take the =Big Five= quiz cold before deciding on the book
body: Answer without reading anything first, then see whether the result matches what the author claims.

title: Work out why word error rate flatters some ASR systems
body: WER counts every substitution the same, so "the" for "a" costs as much as dropping a drug name. Read up on the alternatives (semantic error rate, entity-level accuracy) and pick one to run beside WER on twenty of my own recordings.

title: Learn what a vector database actually replaces before comparing products
body: Understand the nearest-neighbour problem first, then look at Pinecone, Qdrant and pgvector.

title: Read the book on tango endings and take proper notes
body: I can dance through a tanda but the last phrase always feels improvised and slightly panicked. Read the chapter on how the music signals a close, and write *what the final two bars tell the leader to do* into the vault, one note per ending type, before I go to practica on Thursday.

title: Read Designing Machine Learning Systems against my own pipelines
body: Go chapter by chapter and note where Huyen's advice matches what broke for me in production.

title: Map the interpretability landscape by the question each method answers
body:
Every time I read a paper I lose track of what kind of explanation it is actually giving. Build one page sorted by question, not by method name:
- Intrinsic vs post-hoc: is the model itself readable, or am I explaining it afterwards?
- Local vs global: one prediction, or the whole model's behaviour?
- *Which method answers which question* — SHAP, LIME, PDP, counterfactuals, probes, attribution to training data
- Note what each one cannot tell me, especially anything causal

title: Book: Crime and Punishment, in the Pevear and Volokhonsky translation
body: I have been meaning to read a proper Russian novel instead of only reading about them. It is around 550 pages, so aim for =30= pages a day and finish in under three weeks. Read the translation notes first, since translator choice changes the whole feel.

title: Fix the CV PDF so the eye lands on job titles first
body: Make the *job titles and dates* the strongest element on each entry, with lighter body text.

title: Swap ReLU for GELU in a tiny MLP and plot gradients
body: Same seed, same data, and plot per-layer gradient norms to see whether the *activation actually changes the gradient flow*.

title: Finish the practical generative AI book chapters on diffusion
body: Do the diffusers chapters with the code actually run, not just read. [[obsidian:Hands-On Generative AI Notes]]

title: Sketch a side project ranking financial news headlines by relevance
body: Start with a small labelled set of earnings-related text and compare a simple baseline against an embedding model.

title: Start a decision journal for architecture choices at work
body: Record the options, the reasoning and my confidence in each call, then revisit after three months.

title: Learn Python decorators including functools.wraps and arguments
body: I copy decorator snippets without seeing why there are three nested functions once arguments appear. Write a /timing decorator/ with an optional argument, then inspect the function name and docstring with and without functools.wraps to see what gets lost.

title: Work out why TD(0) bootstraps and still converges
body: Rederive the TD(0) update on a five-state random walk before trusting it. [[obsidian:TD learning notes]]

title: Separate aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty with a small ensemble experiment
body:
I use the two words loosely and would not be able to say which one a given model output is capturing. Fix that with a tiny regression problem where the noise level changes across the input range and there is a gap in the middle with no training data at all.

Train a five-member ensemble where each member predicts a mean and a variance. Average predicted variances to get the aleatoric part, and take the variance of the member means as the epistemic part. What I expect: aleatoric follows the noise pattern everywhere, while *epistemic blows up only inside the gap* and shrinks with more data. If the two are tangled, that is the interesting result and the thing to understand.

Then repeat with a single network trained by plain MSE and note what it cannot tell me. Save the plots and a paragraph in the notebook, and try explaining the distinction to myself without using the word reducible.

title: Decide whether lock-free queues and Bayesian optimization are worth it
body: I keep reaching for clever techniques because they are interesting, and lock-free queues are the worst offender. Before building one, write down what the mutex version costs at the contention I actually have: measure it with a realistic thread count and see whether the lock even shows up in a profile. If it is under a few percent of runtime, the answer is no and the note says so. Do the same exercise for Bayesian optimization on the tuning job: count evaluations, how long each takes, and whether a plain random search with the same budget gets within noise of the best result.

title: Profile where a Python script's RAM actually goes
body: A data-loading script uses several times the size of its input file and I have only guessed at why. Run it under tracemalloc, take two snapshots around the parse step, and compare the top ten lines. Also print sys.getsizeof for a small dict and a list of ints to see the per-object overhead.

title: Look up my tetanus and shingles vaccination status
body: Ask the surgery for my vaccine record and check whether a tetanus booster or the shingles jab is due.

title: Read Sutton and Barto properly, but only the first third
body: The canonical reinforcement learning textbook is free and I keep citing it without having read past the bandit chapter. The introductory part is where the ideas actually live: bandits, MDPs, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo, temporal-difference learning. Past that it turns into a reference for when I need a specific method. Do chapters one to six in order, do the exercises that look hard rather than the ones that look pleasant, and write a paragraph per chapter from memory before moving on. If I cannot write the paragraph, I did not read the chapter.

title: Add a =BatchNorm= versus LayerNorm run to the small net
body: Same net, same seed, only the normalization changed; plot loss and gradient norm together.

title: Curate a scored QA set from an open corpus and show the lift
body: Take a large open QA or web-text corpus and score each example with a cheap quality signal: a small classifier, answer-length sanity checks, and deduplication against the test split. Keep the top slice, then fine-tune the same small model on the top slice and on a random slice of equal size. The deliverable is a single table with both runs on one held-out eval, with seeds repeated. If the *curated slice does not beat random by more than the seed noise*, the scoring is not doing anything and I should say so plainly.

title: Send a first real patch to a library I use every week
body: I lean on the same HTTP client library almost daily and have never given anything back, even though I have hit three papercuts in its docs. Read CONTRIBUTING, pick one small documentation or error-message fix from the issue tracker, and open the pull request. Start with the issue about =retry backoff= wording.

title: Implement BPE from scratch on a tiny corpus
body: Tokenizers are a black box I depend on daily. Write the merge loop in about forty lines of Python, train on one text file, and compare the vocabulary against WordPiece's likelihood-based merge rule.

title: Derive EM for a Gaussian mixture by hand, then check against scikit-learn
body: I keep using =GaussianMixture= as a black box and could not explain the M-step if asked. Derive the E and M updates once on paper, write a bare numpy loop for two clusters, and confirm *it lands on the same likelihood as the library* on a toy set.

title: Work out how on-call for a model service differs from ordinary service on-call
body: A model can be fully up and still be quietly wrong, so latency and error-rate pages are not enough. Read two public postmortems and one on-call guide, then sketch what a runbook entry for a drifting model would need: symptom, check, rollback step, owner.

title: Write down which classical RL failure modes reappear in RLHF runs
body: Reward hacking is the obvious one, but the list should be longer: distribution shift between the policy and the reward model as training moves off the data it was fit on, credit assignment over long sequences with a single terminal reward, exploration collapse when entropy drops early, and off-policy staleness when rollouts lag the learner. For each, put one sentence on how it looks in a training curve, so I can recognise it rather than just name it. Keep the note short enough to reread before starting a new run.

title: Reread the scikit-learn calibration guide with a reliability diagram open
body:
Run every example in =sklearn.calibration= myself instead of skimming the plots.
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html

title: Check the Adam update step by hand for the first =3= iterations
body: Do the bias-corrected moments on a one-parameter quadratic and compare to a library run.

title: Decide what the assistant's memory keeps and what goes to notes
body: Memory holds only stable preferences; plans live in =Projects.org=, and anything older than three months gets flagged for deletion.

title: Get multiple comparisons straight before reading another results table
body: Every paper with twenty metrics and a few bolded wins makes me wonder how many of those wins are noise. Work through the arithmetic of familywise error, then Bonferroni, Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg, and simulate a hundred null comparisons to watch about five come out significant. *The key thing to internalise is that the number of comparisons made counts, not just the ones reported.* Write down a rule for what I do when I compare several model variants on my own data.

title: Understand why AdaBoost keeps improving after training error hits zero
body: I can call the library but could not explain the margin story, which is the reason boosting resists overfitting far longer than it should. Read the margin-based argument, then fit AdaBoost on a small dataset and plot the margin distribution after each round.

title: Work out a latency budget for one full voice agent turn
body:
Everyone quotes "under a second" without saying where the time goes, so I want a budget I can actually check against.
- Split a turn into stages: capture, network, endpointing wait, ASR final, LLM first token, TTS first audio, playback
- Read up on the roughly 200–300 ms gap people leave between turns in conversation, and what happens to /perceived/ quality past 800 ms
- Note which stages can overlap by streaming and which are hard serial
- Put the whole thing in a small table with a target and a worst case per stage

title: Skim the Hydra docs and convert one experiment to it
body:
Replace the argparse block in my toy trainer and run a three-value learning rate sweep.
https://hydra.cc/docs/intro/

title: Derive logistic regression from the likelihood and read the odds ratios
body:
I keep quoting odds ratios from model output without being able to say where they come from, which is a bad habit when a colleague asks whether a coefficient of 0.4 is big. Start from the Bernoulli likelihood, write the log-likelihood, take the gradient and show it reduces to X^T(y - p). Note why there is no closed form and that Newton's method turns into iteratively reweighted least squares.

Then the practical half: exponentiate a coefficient, say what it means holding the other predictors fixed, and why it is not a change in probability. Work one example by hand with a binary predictor such as a customer being on a discount plan, then check it against a fitted model on a toy dataset. Finish by writing down what happens to the estimates under perfect separation, because that is the failure I have actually hit and could not explain.
[[obsidian:Logistic Regression Derivation and Odds Ratios]]

title: Read up on *context isolation* for long-running LLM agents
body: Sub-agents with their own windows keep the main thread clean.

title: List the MoE variants worth knowing and what each fixes
body: Switch, GShard, Mixtral-style top-2 routing: one line each on the load-balancing trick.

title: Collect the cases where a plain A/B test beats a fancy bandit
Survey the main kinds of AI agents and how they talk to each other
body: The word agent is used for everything from a chat loop with one tool to multi-party workflows, and I cannot place most of what I read. I want a rough taxonomy, plus a look at MCP and the agent-to-agent protocols to see what problem each one solves. Write a one-page comparison and note which of them I would actually reach for.

title: Review the reading-tracker project area by area before new features
body: The reading tracker has grown by accretion and I keep wanting to add features on top of rough edges. Go through it one area at a time: import code, data model, the stats page, tests, and the README. For each, write down what is confusing or fragile, fix the worst three things, and only then look at the feature list again. No new features until every area has had one pass, even if that pass is only deleting dead code and adding a couple of missing tests.

title: Research a travel monopod versus a tiny tripod for the camera
body: I keep wanting steadier shots at dusk and in dim interiors, but a full tripod is never coming on a trip. Two realistic options: a tabletop tripod that folds to the size of a pen, or a walking-pole style monopod that doubles as something useful. Things to compare: packed length, weight, whether the head is ball or fixed, and whether it would even hold the camera's little body without wobbling. Also the legality question, since some museums and viewpoints ban anything with legs. Stick to =under 300 g= as the hard limit and read a couple of long-term reviews rather than the launch-week ones.

title: Survey open-source TTS models before falling for a demo page
body: Every TTS repo claims to sound human, and half of them turn out to have a non-commercial licence or need a GPU I do not have. Make one table of the open-source candidates — Piper, Coqui XTTS, Kokoro, and whatever is newer — with columns for quality on the same three test sentences, latency to first audio on this laptop, and licence. *Licence goes in the table before I listen to anything*, because a great voice I cannot use is a wasted evening. Use identical text for all of them, including one sentence with numbers and one in the target language.

title: Restart the daily eval-notes habit in =eval-log.org= and hold it three weeks
body: One line per day is enough: what I ran, what number came out, and what surprised me.

title: Plan the shard and replica layout for the main index
body: Right now the whole corpus sits on one node and a rebuild means downtime. Sketch a layout with shard count, replica count and a blue-green rebuild into a fresh alias, using the current =40 GB= index as the sizing baseline, and note what breaks if one shard is lost.

title: Write down a decision rule for tabular deep learning versus GBDT
body: One paragraph I can reuse: dataset size, feature types, latency, and when I would even try a neural net.

title: Work through the Kubeflow Pipelines architecture and its core features
body: I keep using pipeline tools as black boxes and cannot say what the metadata store or the artifact layer actually does. Read the architecture overview, then run the =mnist= sample locally and trace one run from compiled spec to executed pod.

title: Decide how deeply to read the Bayesian data analysis book
body: It is huge and I have been treating it as either everything or nothing. Make a decision: read the first five chapters cover to cover for the basic workflow, then use the rest as a reference when a modelling problem calls for it. Check the free PDF from the author's site so I do not buy the paper copy yet. I will keep a running list in =bda-reading.org= of which chapters I have used for a real problem, and if that list is still empty in three months, the book stays on the shelf.

title: Reproduce Simpson's paradox on the Berkeley admissions numbers
body: I can recite the definition but could not explain *why the aggregate rate reverses once you split by department* without the table in front of me. Load the classic admissions counts into a notebook, compute both views, and write two sentences on which one answers a causal question.

title: List the main bias sources in a recommender's logged data
body: Sampling, position, popularity, selection and exposure bias, with one sentence each on where the bias enters the pipeline.

title: Trace the path from seq2seq with attention to the transformer
body: I know the endpoints but not the steps between them. Read Bahdanau attention, then Luong's variant, then the transformer paper, and note at each step what problem was being solved: the fixed-size bottleneck, then sequential computation. End with a short timeline of design choices such as positional encoding and layer norm placement.

title: Pick the math foundations book for data science and start it
body:
Linear algebra and probability are where my understanding is thinnest, so one focused book beats three half-read ones. Shortlist:
- Mathematics for Machine Learning by Deisenroth, Faisal and Ong (free PDF, =mml-book.com=)
- Introduction to Linear Algebra by Strang
- All of Statistics by Wasserman

title: Build a nightly pipeline that fetches new papers, filters, and mails a digest
body:
Small project, on purpose: a scheduled job that pulls new items from a feed of preprints, drops anything that does not match a short keyword and author list, stores what survives in SQLite, and emits one plain-text digest each morning. The temptation is to start with the ranking model; do not. Version one is fetch, dedupe by ID, filter by keywords, write a row, print a digest. That alone will show whether the feed is worth reading.

Decisions to make up front: cron or a systemd timer, where the state lives so a missed night does not lose items, and how the digest is delivered (email to myself is fine). Log every run with counts of fetched, kept and dropped, because the silent failure mode of these things is a filter that quietly matches nothing for three weeks and I never notice.

Only after a fortnight of real digests, look at whether embeddings or a small classifier would beat the keyword list. [[obsidian:Paper Digest Pipeline Design]]

title: Work through the SIGIR tutorial on unbiased learning to rank
body: The tutorial slides are the fastest route to the propensity-weighting story without reading ten papers in the wrong order. Go through it once with the notebook open, and note where the click model assumptions are actually stated versus hidden. [[obsidian:Unbiased LTR reading list]]

title: Check the =streaming-plus= receipts to see what I actually pay
body: Search the inbox for the last six charges and cancel if the price crept up.

title: Study context isolation for long-running agents using sub-agents
body: Long agent runs rot because the context fills with old tool output. Read how isolating work into sub-agents with clean windows helps, then sketch where I would split a =research-then-write= task.

title: Add micronutrient tracking to the food log beyond just calories
body: Right now the app knows calories and macros and nothing else, so I cannot tell whether I am low on iron or magnesium. Start with just five nutrients, add columns to =foods.db= for them, and fill values for the twenty foods I eat most often before trying to import a full database.

title: Browse the seaborn gallery and steal a few diagnostic plots
body: Pick three plots that would have caught my last training bug and add them to the notebook template.

title: Survey GPU-resident RL simulators and pick one testbed
body: Most of my RL time goes on waiting for CPU environments, so look at Isaac Gym-style, Brax and MJX options and compare them. *Pick one* by how quickly a simple locomotion task trains on a single consumer card, then commit to it for a month before looking at others.

title: Learn what PPO actually fixes compared with vanilla policy gradient
body: I keep quoting the clipped objective without being able to say what instability it is patching. Read the PPO paper alongside the TRPO one, then write half a page on how the clip approximates a trust region and what still goes wrong when the clip range is too loose.

title: Learn to read learning curves before I blame the model again
body: Last two runs I decided the architecture was wrong when the curves were probably telling me something simpler. Collect four examples of each pattern: train loss falling while validation climbs, both plateauing high, validation noisier than train because the split is tiny, and a suspicious gap that appears from epoch one which usually means leakage or a label problem. Plot my own past runs next to them and write one line per run on what I should have checked first. Keep the page short enough that I will actually open it mid-training.

title: Sketch a threat model for the note-summarising agent
body: It reads my inbox, opens links and can send mail, which is all three legs of the risky combination at once. Draw the data flows on one page, mark where untrusted text enters, and decide which permission to drop first. [[obsidian:Agent safety notes]]

title: File the leftover reading items into the right topic notes
body: There are about six saved links on offline evaluation and bandits sitting in the inbox with no home. Open each one, write a one-line summary, and move it into the matching topic note in the knowledge base. Delete the ones I know I will not read.

title: Look at a small travel air purifier for hotel rooms
body: Check whether a pocket-sized unit is *actually worth the weight* or just a gadget that fills a bag corner.

title: Fit a scaling law to my own small runs without fooling myself
body:
I have a dozen training runs at different sizes and the curve looks like a clean power law on a log-log plot, which is exactly when I should be suspicious. Straight lines on log-log plots are forgiving, and a fit with three free parameters through eight points can look convincing and extrapolate badly.

First decide what is fitted and what is held out: fit on the smaller runs, predict the largest two, and report the miss. Include an irreducible-loss term and see how much the exponent changes when it is fixed at zero versus free. Fit with several random starts, since the optimiser is fussy here, and give a rough interval by bootstrapping over runs. If the interval on the exponent is wide enough that the extrapolation is meaningless, that is the result, and I should write it down as such instead of quietly dropping the plot.

title: Give the agent a scoped tool set for the notes vault

title: Check the evidence for role prompting and multi-turn degradation

I keep quoting KV cache numbers from memory and they are always off by some factor I cannot explain. Do it properly once for a concrete case: a 32-layer model with 8 KV heads under grouped-query attention, head dimension 128, fp16, and then a workload of 20 concurrent users with 6k tokens of context each. The formula is two tensors (K and V) times layers times KV heads times head dim times bytes times tokens, so write it out symbolically first and only then plug in numbers.

After that, vary one thing at a time. What happens with full multi-head attention instead of GQA, with an 8-bit cache, with context doubled to 12k? Put the results in a small table and note how many concurrent sessions fit on a 24 GB card once the weights are subtracted. The point is to be able to answer, in under a minute and without a calculator app, whether a given model and traffic pattern is memory-limited by weights or by cache. Also check what paged allocation changes: it does not shrink the cache, it reduces waste from over-reserved contiguous blocks, and I should be able to say roughly how much waste that is.

title: Write a one-page results summary to give my manager before calibration
body:
Calibration happens in a room I am not in, so whatever my manager says about me is limited to what they remember and what I have made easy to repeat. Right now that is probably the last six weeks and one incident. A one-page summary handed over ahead of time fixes the recency problem, and it also forces me to find out whether I can actually state my year in five sentences.

Structure it as four or five results, each with the same three parts: what the problem was, what I did specifically (not what the team did), and the evidence, meaning a number, a design doc, a before-and-after, or a person who would confirm it. Leave out effort and busyness entirely; nobody in calibration scores hours. Include one result that was messy or only partly successful and say what I learned, because a page with no rough edges reads as unreliable. Keep it to one side of paper so it can be pasted into an email without being trimmed.

Then ask for fifteen minutes with my manager a week before the deadline, not the day before, and ask two questions: is anything here likely to be disputed, and what would they add? Their answers matter more than the page. Adjust the summary after that conversation and not before it.

title: Make window functions and CTEs automatic instead of looked-up
body:

The fix is repetition on a small set of shapes, not reading more documentation.

Use one small made-up orders table so the data stops being a distraction and only the syntax is being tested.

The part I usually get wrong is the default frame when there is an ORDER BY inside OVER, which quietly changes what last_value returns. Write a query that demonstrates it, so it is remembered as a bug I have seen rather than a rule I have read. Time each pattern; anything over three minutes goes back on the list for tomorrow. title: Work out GPU autoscaling and what a cold start really costs
body:
Scaling a GPU pool up on demand sounds like a solved problem until you count what happens between a pod being pending and the first token being served. The node has to be provisioned, the driver and device plugin have to come up, the image has to be pulled, and the weights have to be loaded into memory. For a large model that chain can take many minutes, and that is the number that decides whether scaling from zero is acceptable or just embarrassing.

Start by reading how the cluster autoscaler and a queue-based or request-based autoscaler differ, and what signal each one scales on. CPU utilization is a poor signal for GPU work, so look at queue depth or requests in flight instead. Then time a real cold start on the test cluster, broken into node ready, image pulled, weights loaded and first response, so I can see which stage dominates.

After that list the trade-offs plainly: keep one warm replica and pay for idle hours, scale from zero and accept the delay, or pre-pull images and cache weights on local disk to shrink the gap. Decide which fits a bursty workload with a tolerable wait of about a minute, and write down the cost of the warm option per day so the choice is a number instead of a preference.

title: Write a custom iterator class and compare it to a generator
Read Sutton and Barto's RL book, introductory chapters only
body: Every reinforcement learning tutorial I have followed leans on vocabulary I only half own: value functions, bootstrapping, the difference between on-policy and off-policy. title: Sort out time-to-first-token versus inter-token latency for real workloads
body: I keep quoting TTFT and inter-token latency as if they were interchangeable, and they are not: TTFT is dominated by queueing plus prefill, inter-token latency by decode batch size and memory bandwidth. A chat UI cares about both, a summarisation job cares about neither and only about total tokens per second. Pick the two workloads I actually run, decide which metric each one should be judged on, and note the percentile that matters (p95 rather than mean, since the tail is where users notice). Then run a small load test against a local vLLM instance, saved as =latency_sweep.py=, at three concurrency levels and plot how each metric moves as concurrency rises. The point is to see the trade-off in my own numbers rather than in a vendor chart.

title: Trace the Stable Video Diffusion pipeline from pixels to pixels

title: Build a retraining job that only promotes a better model
body:
Right now retraining is a notebook I run when I remember, and whatever comes out overwrites the previous model. That is backwards. *The job must promote a new model only if it beats the current one on the held-out set*, and otherwise leave production alone and log why.

Smallest version that counts: a script that trains, evaluates against the model currently marked as production in the registry, and compares one metric with a small margin so noise does not cause flip-flopping. If it wins, register it and move the alias; if not, exit cleanly. Then run it from a Kubernetes CronJob or a scheduled cloud pipeline on a tiny dataset so a full run takes minutes, not hours.

Things to decide up front: which metric, what margin, and what happens when the evaluation data itself changes. Run it three times, once with a deliberately worse model, to see the rejection path actually work. Turn the schedule off when done so it does not keep spending money.

title: Benchmark the nearest-neighbour index on my own vectors
body: Published ANN benchmarks use clean datasets that look nothing like my embeddings. Sample a hundred thousand of my own vectors, build exact ground truth by brute force, and plot recall against queries per second for HNSW and IVF settings. Report latency percentiles, not the mean.

title: Choose the alert threshold by cost of errors, not by round numbers
body:
The current fraud-score cutoff of 0.5 was never chosen; it was the default and nobody questioned it. A missed case and a false alarm do not cost the same, and the reviewer queue can only absorb so many alerts a day, so the threshold is a budget decision as much as a statistical one.

Write down three numbers first: what a missed positive costs, what a wasted review costs in analyst minutes, and how many reviews per day the team can actually do. Then plot expected cost against threshold on the validation set and mark where the alert volume crosses capacity. *If the cost-optimal threshold produces more alerts than the team can review, the capacity limit wins and the cutoff moves up*, however unpleasant the missed-case number looks.

After that, check how stable the choice is: bootstrap the validation set and see how far the optimum wanders. If it wanders a lot, pick the flatter region of the curve rather than the exact minimum, and re-run the whole exercise each quarter when base rates shift.

title: Decide what safety kit goes in the pack for solo day hikes
body: I walk alone more often now and my kit is a plaster and optimism. The decision is what is actually worth carrying on a day route with patchy signal: a proper foil bivvy rather than a blanket, a whistle, a small headtorch, a paper map and compass I can use, and a charged power bank. A personal locator beacon costs more but is the only item that works with no signal at all, so price one against how often I really go beyond coverage. Also leave a route and return time with someone every time. Pack the kit once, weigh it, and check the batteries on the first of each month. [[obsidian:Hiking safety kit]]

title: Deploy the sentiment model on kind and reach it through a Service
body: Everything I have deployed so far lived in a notebook or behind a managed button, so I could not tell you what a Deployment actually does when a pod dies. Spin up a =kind= cluster, containerise the small sentiment classifier, apply a Deployment with two replicas and a ClusterIP Service, then port-forward and hit it with curl. Kill a pod by hand and watch the replacement arrive. **The point is seeing the Service keep answering while pods churn**, not getting a pretty endpoint. Afterwards delete the cluster with =kind delete cluster= and check that no stray containers are left running in Docker, because forgotten local clusters quietly eat laptop RAM for weeks.

title: Work out when ML is the wrong tool and rules would do
body: Before reaching for a model, I want a checklist that makes me say why a handful of rules or a lookup table would not be enough. Cases to think through: a fraud flag with three known patterns, a ticket router with ten stable categories, a spam filter. For each, ask how often the rules would change, whether there is labelled data at all, and what a wrong answer costs. Also keep in mind that a heuristic is /a baseline you must beat/, not something to skip, so the plan is to write the rules version first and measure it. Two pages of notes is enough, ending with my own decision rule of thumb.
